sentences.text: Yeah, I'm good, thank you.
This meeting is being recorded.
Have you got Samuel coming as well or is it just me?
Yeah, yeah, he will be joining me.
Like physically is here.
So two minutes.
All right, no worries.
Whereabouts you based?
We're based in Tel Aviv usually, but right now we're in Austria visiting the family.
Oh, are you in the countryside?
Yeah, yeah.
What about you?
Yeah, in London, but the, the team is, is actually spread across the Middle East.
London, New York, San Francisco.
So nice how, how big you are.
Sorry?
Like how many people are in the team?
Six of us.
So not particularly big, but six working full time.
Nice.
Okay, so Sammy is coming in a few seconds.
Okay, well we're probably good to begin.
If he's in the room, you can hear.
Yay.
Hi sir.
Hi.
How you doing?
Lovely, thank you.
Having a good Hanukkah?
Yes, it's pretty nice.
We had a big celebration.
Was it yesterday?
No, the day before, on Wednesday.
That must have been good if you can't remember which day it was.
No.
And my, my siblings came from different cities and then we had a lovely little celebration and now we're spending the, the holidays with my family.
Okay, brilliant.
Yeah.
Well, just a little bit about us.
So we are Capital A, we're an M A advisory.
We work exclusively with marketing services companies.
So mostly agencies but also other stuff around that.
So a little bit around the data side of Things and some SaaS and software businesses as well.
But it's usually marketing or media related, pretty much 100% actually what we're doing is marketing stuff.
We have agencies co as well, which is a marketplace for agency owners to buy and sell agencies.
And in fact the one that I mentioned, which was a Tel Aviv based influencer company, Leaders Group they're called, we just sold them to an American company, a listed American company.
So yeah, we, we are active in Israel as well.
We've actually got a couple of clients that are on board and at the moment they're Israeli companies too.
So lots going on.
I was just saying as well, we, we.
I'm based in, in London but we have team team members based in the Middle east and in New York and San Francisco.
So we're spread out.
Most of our business is US based.
It'd be good to find a little bit about you guys and what scale ups does and what it is that you're trying to achieve and whether we can help you.
Yeah.
Can I ask a question just a bit before?
Yeah, sure.
What are your thoughts regarding like the.
The situation in Israel, like involving the, involving the geopolitical stuff.
That.
Yeah.
Situation that we have.
Yeah.
And how it affects, you know, buying and selling agencies or generally doing business between international companies and Israeli companies because you have like Israeli customers.
So I'm interested to understand if they're like more investors now or less or if the Americans are holding off or you know how.
Yeah, so, so the deal we did with, with Stagwell and Leaders Group, that was in, I think it was August time so everything.
The war was in full swing at that point.
I don't believe that we had any less interest because it was an is Israeli based company.
I, I do believe that the owner of Stagwell is Jewish, he's an American, but I don't know whether that was a, a factor or not.
I really don't know.
So it could be that actually there's more involvement from American businesses trying to buy into Israel anyway because they're actively supporting Israel.
So.
But, but in regards to, to us.
So we started the process with Leaders Group probably around November, December time last year.
So it was about a seven or eight month process overall.
And you know, there was, there was active, you know, battles, war going on at that point all the way through the, the entire process.
So obviously there will be people that are for and against what's going on and you know it's, I think it will accelerate some interest and it will decrease other interests.
But I think generally speaking it's not necessarily a bad time.
I think the founder of Leaders actually might be working from Dubai now.
So I don't know whether he's still in Tel Aviv or not, whether he took some money and went on holiday.
But yeah, I mean, how are you finding it business wise?
I mean internationally from a business perspective, are things slowing down for you or have they not really changed?
Actually no, not at all.
But, but I don't know, like, you know, people speak and we hear, we hear one side and like the other side.
So I was just like interested to understand like how you see.
And the business of Leaders Group was that mainly Israeli clients or mostly international?
Well, so Stagwell said that they were interested in them as a company because they were a gateway into the Middle East.
So I think there was a mix of international clients as well as some Middle Eastern companies that they were dealing with.
But you know, brands are mostly international, aren't they?
So they're looking to work with companies both internationally and in local markets.
Yeah, so.

And I think just on your point Rosie, I, I think that there are just, there's probably like you, you're hearing two sides of the story and in the UK as well there's very much sort of pro Palestinian sentiment, there's lots of marches on the streets.
But equally I think you know there's a huge amount of support for Israel as well, you know, so I think it's, it's just two sides and where wherever you look you'll find both sides of that story.
Yes.
Yeah.
So yeah, I, I think there is interest definitely in what you're doing.
You, you're dealing with a lot of tech companies as well, I understand.
So a lot of those will already be based in Israel because obviously have a very good correct.
So.
So maybe I can give you a bit of background on on scale ops and sort of a quick rundown.
So it's I think between right now it's a 12 person company but it always shifts.
Sometimes it's 14 people, sometimes it's 11 and I think right now it's going to be more towards 15 in Q1.
The company itself, it's a bit different from other agencies in that it's a rev ops outsourcing company mainly.
So we basically provide revenue operation services as a service to tech companies.
Typical clients are 30 plus scale ups and enterprise.
But I would say mostly you could think of, you know, Monday could be a client cyber reason.
All those sort of multi hundred people Israeli tech companies about 80% of the clients are in Israel, 20% are international.
Some of them are like Israeli American tech scale ups and some of them are purely abroad.
Like one, I think we have a few clients in the US now, one in UK and we had a one in the Netherlands as well.
We manage about 10 to 15 clients simultaneously so we don't really have a huge dependency on any one client per se.
And what they buy is really full time or part time positions.
So they pay the, the premium for having the best practices and having the, the knowledge from the, on the revenue operations.

But they, it's effectively outsourcing and then the, and so we don't commit like it's not project based but it's ongoing retainers mostly we don't do any more really implementations and things like that.
But it's, it's like the, the step.
It'S a foot in the door.
Yeah, that's the small portion of the company.
It's like we have also the licenses that we're getting either from Salesforce or HubSpot or whatever like tool we are working with.
And so we do that and we've been for the first two, three years we were very HubSpot focused as an agency or as a company.
And now we are sort of supporting the entire tech stack of the, of the client.

So for example, if the client uses outreach to do email marketing and then he uses HubSpot to do the CRM and then he uses, I don't know, zoom info for the database and he uses Air Call for his, for his voiceover IP calls and things like that, then the revenue operations person that we would provide takes care of the entire stack.
So meaning that for example, if you do a zoom webinar, that the data flows into HubSpot, that the emails get sent out via outreach, et cetera, et cetera.
Yeah, usually the core Systems or the CRM or the ERPs, like CRM.
ERP is like HubSpot Salesforce usually for the bigger companies, HubSpot for marketing, Salesforce for sales and service.
And then there is like a whole dozens of other tools that are integrated that we support as well.
So our role is not only to support the CRM or to support HubSpot, although we are HubSpot and Salesforce partner.
It just like to support, get them through the old funnel, the old revenue funnel lead to cash, the old journey.
So we're, and we don't do any communications, so meaning that, I mean we have a marketing person on our team that supports clients if they need like a, a webinar, like a brand thing or something.
But we're not a branding agency and not a PR or advertising or communications.
So we don't do like their website design or, or things like that.
And in terms of sort of size and, and growth.
So we, I don't know how much you're aware, but in 21 and during COVID Israel had a huge tech boom.
So we had sort of a huge growth in, in the, in revenue and profitability during 22 and then now with the, actually it started before the war with the judicial reform and things like that.
So the tech sector, I think globally, but especially also in Israel, slowed down.
So we saw that also in our business and now we're seeing it pick up again.
So if you look at the last three financial years, you had like one peak in 22 and then some decline and steady from there and now growing again.
Okay, so what do those numbers look like across those four years, including this year.
Sorry, sorry, what's this question?
What was your revenue?
If you can give me the revenue number.
So I can see we're talking about.
We'Re talking about around 1.5 to 2.
Million revenue a year.
Okay, so you peaked 2 million.
It depends which year.
But yeah, like there were like, we.
Only started in 2020, so we really have like 2021, 2022 and 2023 to compare.
What about this year?
Are you back above 1.5 or still around the.
The what, sorry, are you at 1.5 million in revenue?
This year was a bit lower.
This was.
This year was around 1.2.
Do you know what your margin is?
Has it stayed the same across those four years or have you.
The margin was higher at the beginning.
It was around like we had an EBITDA of like around 50%.
Wow.
Yeah.
And then we hired more senior people to the team, so we had like, of course, more expense as it went to like around 30 this year.
This year was the lowest, but it was like around 20, I think.
But still it's like, good.
Okay, all right, cool.
So.
So what is it that you guys are looking to achieve?
What do you, what do you want to do?
Is it because you need a larger platform to work with to grow, or are you looking to get out?
I mean, what's, what's the strategy?
So I think, I think maybe I can only speak for myself, but I think from this, Rose is running the company day to day as CEO.
Right.
And I think we've seen sort of what we want to get out of this.
Sort of every year looks the same kind of trajectory.

So in the way that, you know, one client goes and another client comes and sort of we stay in the Israeli market and our revenue is between 1.2 and 1.8 and you know, profitability is between 20 and 40%, I think, and, and what we want to.
And we would like to go get out of that.
We bought an Agency in 22 in.
In Israel, but mainly for the commissions and we didn't take any staff and we had, we took on some clients that were theirs and we tried to buy an agency last year in the UK or.
And it was about five month process and ultimately it didn't work out.
So we learned a lot about what not to do, not necessarily how to do it right.
But I think we have, I think what we would like to have is sort of a one to three year plan of how to grow the sort of.
I think in three years time probably Rose would probably like to do something else or in two years.
So I think ultimately what we would like to do is ideally get the, the best band for the money and grow in a.

Like, if it makes sense to grow geographically, we would probably like to, to do that and if that's more attractive to a potential acquirer for us to be active in the UK or in the us we would be open to do that both organically, but I think we are finding that we're limited in that sense, but rather maybe inorganic maybe to, to buy an agency and then to be bought in, in two years from now.
But I think ideally to have sort of an exit strategy on a two or three year horizon, I think that's more or less.
And, and to think about what that trajectory should look like.
Should it just be to maximize profitability now and then, you know, sell.
That's also an option.

But I think we know a little bit the Israeli buyers, so we know sort of our part like agencies that are around us or maybe some groups that are maybe stronger in salesforce but don't have a strong HubSpot leg.

So, you know, there's maybe five players or so in Israel that could be relevant, but whether we would at least like to know what's, what's out there internationally before we speak properly with them.
Does that make sense, Andy, does that answer your question?
Yeah, it does, yeah.
I mean, so basically all options are on the table at the moment.
It's, nothing's decided.
You're looking at your options so well in terms of where you're at.
So you haven't really grown.
It's, it's kind of flat, isn't it?
You know, there was a tech boom and then there was a tech bust.
Everybody was laying off tech stuff in California and explode down all of the marketing as well for everybody.
So you've kind of experienced what everybody on a global scale has experienced.
Right.
But it doesn't, it doesn't really put you on your best foot forward.
Obviously your margins are decreasing as you build the team and that happens with companies as they mature.
So that's really normal, particularly if you're in tech and marketing because you're able to get those really great margins when there's two people running the company at the start.

But obviously you realize you need people to do the service and you build that team up and your margins come down and then finally you put in management to do everything for you and your margins really.

And I think we also overstaffed a little bit during the tech boom and weren't necessarily aware of how much we are in a bubble, or you could say bubble, but I think we, we went, we hired probably three or four people too many and that like for six to 12 months and that put our profitability significantly down when we maybe if we had been more aware of how special the macroeconomic situation is, we could have maybe done it more defensively, if that makes sense.
Yeah, I mean you, you obviously need to move quickly if, if you're on the other side of a bubble and get rid of staff to get you to your cost tank and stuff are obviously the, the biggest cost base.

So I mean what, what is your preferred option is, is because obviously you're looking at a timeline of two to three years and obviously if you were acquired today there would be some level of earn out.
Usually it's a two or three year process.
So that would give Rosie that three years for her to finish what she's doing, maybe build within a large company and then exit.

But you're not going to sell for the best price today you'll probably get a better multiple because actually when we're buying for clients we don't look for companies with 50% margins, we look for companies with 20, 25% margins because that means it's a more mature business with a management team and if you do go separate ways from the, the founders, the management team can take over the running on the, the day today.
So the multiples are probably going to be better because of that.
But obviously your ebitda, you know that number that we're working with is.
Like.
Is that the multiple number that's being taken in?
Yeah.
So we're going to look at your EBITDA and we'll multiply it.
So a business that is your size, generally speaking 3-5x I think you're going to get maybe a better multiple for several reasons.
One issue in the tech space, another is you're working with HubSpot which is very popular.
I mean we did a campaign across the the EU look for HubSpot, diamond and above partners to, to acquire for a company in the UK so that there is value to that.
Plus you're working with clients on a retainer basis and not project basis, et cetera, et cetera.
So there's a few things that will probably put you at the top end of that mult.
So I would say maybe 5x on 240 is probably a current valuation somewhere between 4, 4 and 5.
I would say I'd be pretty confident with that as a, as a sort of starting point but obviously as in terms of an exit for you guys, that's not anything to get too excited.
I mean there's nothing wrong with, with that at all.
But also the way the Tax system works in Israel.

I think you probably get taxed on day one for the entire investment that a company was, was going to make even though you didn't take the money for you know, maybe another year or, or two with the, the actual earn out as well.
So it's probably not the best situation for you guys.
I should imagine you were hoping to get a lot more a couple of million at the start and then an earn out with a couple of million in the bank.
So it's probably better, better for you to, to spend the next six to 12 months getting the company in a position where you will have that maybe slightly better multiple.
But I mean it's entirely up to you the way that we work.
So there's a couple of ways that we work.
One is we can work with you through an entire M and a process which I think would be too heavy handed at the moment.
The other is we have Agencies Co as a platform.
You can list yourself on like that platform for completely free.

And then obviously we're, we're managing all of our marketing around the platform and if we find a buyer for you then we will take you through that M and a process if you like them, you know, if you, if you want to do the deal.
So that's kind of risk free approach.

And then we also work on a, we have like a done with you process that's three months long called Agencies X where we work with companies like yourself and get them to a point where they're two or three times more valuable.

And actually part of that process is seeing whether we can get an acquisition done as well because of that multiple arbitrage it's called, I'm sure you're familiar with it but the idea that you can buy something for three or four times multiple and because you're a bigger company immediately becomes worth maybe five or six or seven times multiple.
So that's part of the process as well.
What is it that you're looking to do though?
I mean what's your, your preferred way to go?
I mean I think we feel pretty comfortable about the business that we have and the, the revenue that we'll get and the margins that, that we can even increase them.

So I think we would probably be able like we can already see now we've made some changes over the last quarter and we can see now that we're improving profitability and we can also see that the tech sector is, is bouncing back and that we get bigger, bigger deals again.

So I think for 25 we're looking at like, for our component, like, I don't know if I want to say 20 to 30% growth, but I think that would be our organic sort of growth and then sort of basically taking home the 20 to 30% profitability.
So, and if we do that three years, then that's.
Or four years, that's sort of your, your EBITDA multiple.
Right, I got you correctly.
So I, I think that's the, that's the natural option.
The other one means taking money that you've already earned and putting it at risk again.
And yeah, I think that would require some level of confidence in the fact in that this is actually sort of part of a bigger plan that will lead a much bigger return.
So I think for now, like sort of, you could say we're financially comfortable and we feel, but ultimately right now the equity that we have doesn't have any value.
We haven't put it, we haven't sold part of it, we haven't sold all of it.
So it's a, it's a paper value at best.
And I think like.

But if you tell us right now, sir, so, for example, five times ebitda, a million dollars, it's not a big, it doesn't change our lives in any significant way, shape or form that would probably be, we'd rather keep, you know, the company have a couple hundred K us every year and, and keep it running.
If on the other hand, we're looking at $5 million or even more than probably the, the sales scenario starts to make sense for us, does that, you know.
Yeah, yeah, sure.
So it's probably too early then, by the sounds.
Yeah, by the sounds of things.
And obviously it's a very new business anyway.
You're, you're four years old, five years coming up to five years old.
So there's still, I'm sure, plenty of time to get bored of what it is that you're doing.
But actually I think it possibly is a little bit early because we're just before 2025 and I'm sure that Q1, you're going to start taking on new clients.

But actually the best time to sell is, is when that process, when the flywheel is moving in the right direction and obviously if we can go to market, and I'm just suggesting this, if it's something that you're seriously considering, if we went to market and maybe Q2 or Q3 and things were growing and we were heading back up beyond 1.5 million revenue, then it would be a good, a better time.
You know, you'd be on a stronger foot forward situation.
And also we could look for a buyer that is willing to give you some kind of rollover equity into the holding company.

So usually what it looks like is they acquire 80% of the business, they leave 20% equity in the business for the founders, but obviously everything grows and then over a three year period, your 20% is then worth maybe four or five times more than it's worth.
So you get that second bite and the apple.

But it means you can take some value off the, off the table now, I mean whether that is exciting enough to take a million dollars over the next three years, probably not because you're kind of nearly there anyway.
So yeah, I would, I would suggest that probably that's a, a two or three year play might be the one that would be the most exciting outcome for everybody.
But does that mean.
So as you mentioned, sort of that anyway, the earn out is a two year thing at least.
So we would have to.
Basically it means that the timeline goes back that we now have a year or two to build sort of significant enterprise value, maybe even buy another, buy an agency abroad and things like that.
And to the buying process a year or two from now with then an earn out of two years.
Is that sort of the more or less the, the most, how should you say, attractive scenario from your point of view?
Well, yeah, I mean it all depends, you know, it depends where you are today.
If Rosie wants to get out in, in two years, then a good or two or three years, it's usually a three year earner.
It can be negotiated, sometimes five even.
But obviously when you're a smaller company like your size, you just want to sell, get some, some value off the table and get out as quickly as possible.
What I would say in terms of what Rosie's timeline is, it may be different from yours, I'm not sure, but the best time to start the process would be probably in the next three to six months.
And then as the business grows, we find a buyer and we have a really great story of, you know, the tech sector is, is booming again.
We're on an up cycle at the start of a start of a growth cycle and it would be a good time to buy into the company.

And so we would be looking for a controlling stake of the business, but one that provides you with some rollover equity, gives Rosie an opportunity to move out the business over a period of time and then gives them enough time to hire the next CEO and, and do something else for the long term.
Either put in A CEO that's going to stay with the business as they sell it into a private equity or, or something else.
So, yeah, I mean, it sounds like you've still got a lot to think about.
Hopefully I've given you something to think about.

My personal position would be, if I was in Rosie's seat would be to get the business on its best foot over the next three to six months, try and win some business, get rid of staff that aren't performing or there's just overhead for no reason, try and get that margin as high as possible and then go to market while we're still growing, while we've still got business in the funnel and then we can, we can go to market with a really great story.
People will get excited and you'll get better multiples that way as well.
So it could go beyond that.
I mean, we've had 13 and a half times multiples for businesses as well.
So, I mean, it's a real variation across and it's just about getting the buyers excited so that they want to pay the best price, basically.
So, yeah, that's what it's all about.
And do you see value in that sort of what you see as the key milestones or value inflection points over, over those sort of over one year or even more, where you see sort of.
That the enterprise value could go from a million dollars to two or three or even five.
So, yeah.
So what I would look to do is get your EBITDA as, as good as it can be.
I think you've already got a lot of those characteristics that would give you a good multiple anyway.
But what you're looking for is long contracts with your clients, probably more international contact clients as well.
So you can show more diversification outside of the Israeli market, just in case there was some up and downs on the local level.
Like I said about leaders, they were looked upon as a great gateway from Europe into the Middle east as well.

So it might be worth seeing whether there is more in the Middle east that can be done in terms of growth and if you can make that one more acquisition, which I think considering your track record, you'll probably find the funding fairly straightforward.

You know, if you could, say, borrow 500K and acquire an agency that's doing 1 million in revenue, then that would stand you in good stead in terms of multiples and EBITDA margins as well to go forward, that you're going to get much better situation than you have.
Yeah, super helpful.
Yeah, yeah, super helpful.
What would you recommend as the Next.
Step now, would you list, would you.
Like recommend to be listed in the, in the website as you mentioned?
I mean the question how much I.
Would love you to.
Yeah, I would, but in terms of, I would love it.
I mean we would find buyers for this.
It's a good business and it's in a good, good space on a couple, in a couple of different levels.

But I, you know, if I was you, I think I would try and get through Q1, really build the pipeline for new business back, back up so that we can go to market the start of Q2, maybe Q3, and we can, we can get that transaction timed because it takes about five to six months.
But we want a buyer at the table in about three or four months into the process.

If we have somebody looking to buy and we have them in negotiation, they're interested and you'll get, you're still winning new contracts and you're still building the business, they'll be more and more excited and we can get better, better multiple side if we have another conversation at the end of March.
Yeah, exactly.
By the end of the next quarter.
Yeah, I think so.
And then in terms of like the timing is just right for you then Rose, if you do want to get out in two years.
Because if we go to market, you know, sort of March, April time, it takes about six months to finish the transaction.
So hopefully we'll be sold before Hanukkah next year and then that gives you a two or three year earner and that means you're out of the business, you know, before the end of the decade.
So that would give you a, a good exit.
And then most likely it would be a growing group of, of agencies and they would have a strategy as well that they were going to go to market in a two or three year period.
I mean we sold an agency last year and as soon as the deal was done, the company that bought them got bought a month later.
So, so they were literally out of the deal within a month.
I mean it was a quite magical sort of timing for them.
But the companies that are buying are looking to do that multiple arbitrage as well.
So they're, they're looking to build a portfolio that becomes way more valuable.
And if you can keep a piece of rollover equity in that, that next deal, then it means you can get to sort of, you know, chunks of money on the deal.
Say at the moment it's not very exciting for you guys.
If we could get like a 6x and you had 400k's worth of EBITDA in the, in the pipeline, then that gives us a really strong position to go to market with.
And it's much better.
You know, it's a million in cash up front and that's just a better deal to be negotiating and then you get the rest of the money.
And Andy, would you be able maybe to be in contact with us if you get any other revops agency that wants to be sold as well?
That could be like a good opportunity for us to acquire.
Yeah.
So it could be also like a.
Possibility from our side to acquire a business.
Yeah, sure.

Like you said, I think if we were to find a company that, you know, we could buy for probably less than a million dollars that is either UK or US based and that from your perspective of looking a year or two ahead gives us a much stronger story and we can improve their processes, we can maybe upsell some of their clients.
Like we feel very confident in our management abilities to generate sort of, you could say enterprise value.
And it could be a small team, it can be a three or five people or so company that we then have a strong foothold in another geographic location.
We are not particularly, we haven't really had any business in the rest of the Middle East.
Like, you know, obviously Dubai would be the most natural place.
We haven't done any business with in the Middle east outside of Israel.
Really.
Yes.
But we haven't done anything in Dubai or in Saudi Arabia or in, in Kuwait or anything like that.
If you think that's sort of the, the story that we should tell rather than trying to get into the U.S.
Or I think the U.S.
look, the, the U.S.
and Europe, they love Israeli tech companies.
So if all your clients are, are that currently on 90 of them is, then that's attractive.
You know, why wouldn't an American buyer want to get an agency that's working with a load of upcoming Israeli tech companies?
That makes total sense.
So I'm not saying don't, don't look at that, but what I'm saying is as another string to your bow, you know, having, you know, two or three clients in Dubai is not going to hurt.
Plus there's loads of millionaires are fleeing UK at the moment because of the labor government here to live in Dubai because there's better tax situations as well.
So there is a bigger story than just being the Middle East.
There's a lot of Europeans living in Dubai right now, so, so, so it just could be another extra thing.
But I think you're going to be an attractive business to European and American agencies anyway, as well as maybe more Israeli companies.
But you probably know those those buyers.
Anyway, I'm gonna have to to jump on my thank you so much.
Thank you.
But what I'll do is I'll put you down as a buyer in our CRM so that we can see that you're interested in Rev Rev Ops companies if they become available.
But, but I'll also add a note, put you in as an opportunity and add you as a note to get back to you in mid March, and then let's have a conversation then and see if anything has changed.
But definitely the story needs to be growth, I think, to get the best exit for you.
Thank you.
Thank you so much, Andy.
Super.
Yeah.
Great to meet you both.
Really exciting business.
Yeah.
Let's, let's talk soon.
Have a.
